title: The history of the falling cat
tagline: From a Paris photograph in 1894 to robot dogs: three centuries of asking how a cat turns over on nothing.
intro: Scientists have wondered how cats land on their feet since at least 1700. Marey's 1894 film proved a cat turns over with nothing to push on, which seemed to break the law of angular momentum and set off a debate in Paris. Physiologists, engineers, vets and mathematicians have been unpicking it ever since.

eras.name: Before the camera
eras.summary: Scientists dropped cats and wondered, but nobody could see the turn: it is over in a fraction of a second.

eras.name: The Paris debate
eras.summary: Marey's film showed a cat turning with no spin, and physicists had to restate what conservation of angular momentum really allows.

eras.name: How the body does it
eras.summary: Physiologists traced the reflex to the inner ear, filmed it at high speed and timed how kittens learn it.

eras.name: Astronauts and geometry
eras.summary: The space age turned the cat into an engineering problem, and mathematicians found deep geometry in it.

eras.name: Falls, robots and spines
eras.summary: Vets studied cats that fall from buildings, engineers built robots that land like cats, and anatomists found what makes the cat's spine so twistable.

events.title: First scientific paper on cat-righting
events.text: According to physicist-historian Gregory Gbur, the French scientist Antoine Parent published the first research paper on how cats right themselves in 1700. His explanation was later shown to be wrong.
events.why: It marks the start of a 300-year scientific puzzle.

events.title: Maxwell's 'cat-turning' letter
events.text: Writing to his wife while examining for the Mathematical Tripos, Maxwell joked that Trinity legend said he threw cats out of windows. He explained the real question was how fast a cat turns, and that even dropped onto a bed from about two inches, a cat still lands on its feet. The letter was printed in his 1882 biography.
events.why: Shows top physicists were already puzzling over the trick decades before photography could catch it.

events.title: Muybridge photographs a running cat
events.text: Muybridge's 781-plate Animal Locomotion included plate 717, a cat trotting and breaking into a gallop. It shows sequence photography was ready to capture fast animal motion, though this plate is a running cat, not a falling one.
events.why: Sequence photography set the stage for Marey's falling-cat film.

events.title: Marey films a falling cat for the Academy
events.text: At his Station physiologique in Paris, Marey filmed a cat let go upside down and showed the frames to the Academy of Sciences. They show it starts with no spin, so it cannot have pushed off the hand. It bends, turns its front half with the legs tucked, then the back half, and lands upright.
events.why: Photographic proof that a cat turns over with nothing to push against.

events.title: Guyou explains the mechanics
events.text: Commandant Guyou, a naval officer and Academy member whom Marey credited with the explanation, showed that a body can rotate in steps while its total angular momentum stays zero. Changing which half has the larger moment of inertia makes each twist leave a net turn.
events.why: Showed the 'impossible' flip does not break the law of conservation of angular momentum.

events.title: Maurice Lévy: a cat could flip even in a vacuum
events.text: Lévy noted the question had been raised at the previous session and argued that jointed bodies such as humans and cats can reorient themselves without outside forces. He even described how a person floating in a vacuum could rotate by cycling the legs.
events.why: Generalised the cat trick to any jointed body, including astronauts decades later.

events.title: A gymnast comparison
events.text: At the same session, Mesny pointed out that gymnasts make similar movements while falling vertically.
events.why: An early link between the cat trick and human acrobatics.

events.title: Deprez admits the textbooks were wrong
events.text: Deprez said he had once dropped cats onto a cushion and had urged Marey to photograph them. He granted that the standard textbook statement of the law, as written by many authors, had been too strict, and proposed a device to demonstrate the effect.
events.why: Shows the cat forced physicists to restate a basic theorem more carefully.

events.title: Appell's wheel-and-workers example
events.text: Appell offered a teaching example: workers walking around a frictionless wheel and changing position in four phases can leave the wheel turned, though it started and ended at rest.
events.why: A simple model of how shape changes produce rotation without spin.

events.title: Nature reports the tumbling cat
events.text: The journal Nature printed Marey's frames under the title Photographs of a Tumbling Cat, taking the Paris argument to English-speaking scientists.
events.why: Took the debate to an international English-speaking audience.

events.title: Peano's cat note
events.text: The mathematician Peano published a short explanation of the cat's turn in his Rivista di Matematica. He then applied the same idea to the slow wandering of Earth's rotation pole.
events.why: The cat problem spilled into geophysics.

events.title: Peano and Volterra clash over Earth's wobble
events.text: Peano's paper on the pole shift of the Earth used cat-like internal motions, and Vito Volterra replied in notes to the Turin and Lincei academies. The exchange ran until early 1896.
events.why: An example of a cat puzzle informing a serious planetary-physics debate.

events.title: Stokes's daughter records 'cat-turning'
events.who: Isabella Humphry (Mrs Laurence Humphry); George Gabriel Stokes
events.text: In a memoir of her father, George Gabriel Stokes's daughter recalled that he, like Maxwell at about the same time, was interested in cat-turning: dropping a cat back-down close to the floor to watch it land on its feet.
events.why: Independent evidence that Victorian physicists experimented with falling cats.

events.title: Science asks how a falling cat turns over
events.text: Physicist W. S. Franklin published 'How a falling cat turns over in the air' in Science.
events.why: Shows the puzzle was still live among physicists after Marey.

events.title: Rademaker joins Magnus's posture laboratory
events.who: G. G. J. Rademaker, Rudolf Magnus
events.text: Rademaker joined the Utrecht laboratory where Rudolf Magnus's group studied posture. His surgical skill, helped by his wife Blanche Stoltz's care of the animals, made long experiments possible.
events.why: The Utrecht school became the centre of righting-reflex research.

events.title: Magnus publishes Körperstellung
events.text: Magnus's book on body posture showed that the inner-ear labyrinth is the main sense organ for posture and balance, and catalogued the reflexes that set the body upright.
events.why: It established the neurology behind the righting reflex.

events.title: Bend-and-twist model
events.who: G. G. J. Rademaker, J. W. G. ter Braak
events.text: The Dutch physiologists Rademaker and ter Braak proposed that the cat bends at its middle and rotates its two halves about their own axes. Gbur calls this the most important part of the righting motion.
events.why: Introduced the mechanism later confirmed by computer models.

events.title: Filming a falling cat at 1500 frames a second
events.text: McDonald presented high-speed film of a freely falling cat, shot at 1500 frames per second, to the Physiological Society.
events.why: Gave far finer detail of the twist than Marey's camera.

events.title: Air Force 'Cat Reflex' for astronauts
events.who: Aerospace Medical Research Laboratories (Kulwicki, Schlei, Vergamini)
events.text: An Air Force report, 'Weightless Man: Self-Rotation Techniques', proposed nine ways an astronaut could turn without pushing on anything. The first, called the Cat Reflex, copied falling cats.
events.why: Turned the cat trick into a spaceflight technique.

events.title: Life shows astronauts moving like cats
events.text: Life magazine featured Kane's NASA-funded work, with a trampolinist in a spacesuit copying a falling cat's moves to turn in mid-air.
events.why: Made the cat-astronaut link famous.

events.title: Kane and Scher's two-cylinder cat
events.who: Thomas R. Kane, M. P. Scher
events.text: Kane and Scher modelled the cat as two cylinders joined at the spine that bend and twist without total spin, and showed this matches the turn. NASA funded the work.
events.why: Widely regarded as the first full mechanical solution.

events.title: From cats to astronaut self-rotation
events.text: Kane presented a dynamic analysis linking cat motion to self-rotation manoeuvres for a free-falling astronaut.
events.why: Carried the cat solution directly into space engineering.

events.title: When do newborn kittens learn the trick?
events.text: Yamamoto dropped newborn kittens upside down from 30-40 cm daily for 36 days. Kittens aged 27 days or younger did not right themselves.
events.why: Showed the reflex is not present at birth.

events.title: Air righting matures by five weeks
events.who: J. R. Villablanca, C. E. Olmstead
events.text: Tracking kittens from birth to 120 days, the authors found air righting starts to appear around day 25 and is mature by day 35.
events.why: Gives a widely cited timetable for kitten development.

events.title: Blind kittens right themselves on schedule
events.who: J. Cremieux, C. Veraart, M. C. Wanet
events.text: Kittens blind from birth developed the reflex exactly like sighted kittens, mature by 33 days. The authors concluded the reflex is mainly driven by the inner-ear vestibular system.
events.why: Shows balance organs, not eyes, drive the reflex.

events.title: Mapping kitten postural reflexes
events.text: Sechzer's team scored kittens' reflexes from birth to 7 weeks and found air righting developed by the 5th week, with reflexes maturing from head to tail.
events.why: Confirms the five-week timetable.

events.title: Shapes, gauge fields and swimming
events.text: Shapere and Wilczek described self-propulsion of tiny swimmers as a gauge field over the space of shapes. The same geometry describes how a cat turns by changing shape.
events.why: Connected the cat to modern geometric phase ideas.

events.title: High-rise syndrome in New York cats
events.who: W. O. Whitney, C. J. Mehlhaff
events.text: Two New York vets, W. O. Whitney and C. J. Mehlhaff, described 132 cats treated after falls from buildings over five months. 90% of the treated cats survived, most with chest injuries. Cats killed outright rarely reached the hospital, so the sample leaves them out.
events.why: Real-world data on falling cats, with a survivorship-bias caveat.

events.title: Rats show a central motor program
events.who: Y. Laouris, J. Kalli-Laouri, P. Schwartze
events.text: Studying rat pups, the team found air righting develops between days 8 and 18 even when neck and pelvis twists were blocked. They rejected Magnus's chain-of-reflexes idea for a built-in motor program.
events.why: Challenged the classic explanation of how the brain runs the reflex.

events.title: Gauge theory of the falling cat
events.text: Montgomery analysed the Kane-Scher cat using gauge theory, the mathematics also used in particle physics. The paper appeared in the first volume of Fields Institute Communications, devoted to the falling cat and related problems.
events.why: Made the cat a showcase example of geometric mechanics.

events.title: Cats in weightlessness
events.text: A review of parabolic-flight and space experiments noted that basic vestibular reflexes, such as the cat's righting reflex, may be affected in weightlessness.
events.why: Shows the reflex depends on sensing gravity.

events.title: Greek high-rise cats
events.text: A Greek study of 207 cats (1988-1998) found a mean fall of 3.7 storeys and fractures in half the cats.
events.why: Added European data to the high-rise picture.

events.title: Zagreb: 119 falling cats
events.text: Vets in Zagreb studied 119 cats that fell 2 to 16 storeys; 96.5% survived. Injuries got sharply worse from the 7th storey up.
events.why: Challenged the idea that higher falls are safer.

events.title: A robot cat flips in mid-air
events.text: Kawamura analysed live cats and built a robotic cat that turned 180° in the air and landed upright.
events.why: Showed the cat strategy works in machines.

events.title: Falling Felines and Fundamental Physics
events.text: Physicist Gregory Gbur published a book-length history of the falling cat problem with Yale University Press.
events.why: The first full history of the puzzle.

events.title: Mini Cheetah, the falling cat
events.who: Vince Kurtz, He Li, Patrick Wensing, Hai Lin
events.text: Researchers combined trajectory optimisation and machine learning so the Mini Cheetah robot dog could rotate in mid-air and land on its feet, from starting pitch angles of -90 to 90 degrees.
events.why: Cat-style righting for legged robots.

events.title: The cat's twisty upper spine
events.text: Tests on cat spines found the chest section twists far more easily than the lower back, with a 47° 'free play' zone. High-speed film showed the front half finishes turning first.
events.why: New anatomical support for the front-first, sequential model.

series.caption: Most cats in these studies fell three to six storeys.

facts: In 1870 Maxwell wrote that a cat dropped onto a bed from about two inches still landed on its feet.
Marey's 1894 frames show the cat starts with no spin, so it cannot have pushed off the hand that let it go.
Kittens blind from birth develop the air-righting reflex on the same timetable as sighted kittens.
In a 2026 study, the front half of a falling cat finished turning before the back half, helped by a very twistable chest spine.
Mathematicians use the falling cat as a textbook example of a geometric phase, the same idea that describes swimming microbes.
